choices.text: A neutral, highly reactive molecule containing a divalent carbon
A positively charged ion containing a trivalent carbon
choices.why: That is a carbocation. A carbene is neutral and its carbon is divalent.

choices.text: A negatively charged ion with three groups on carbon
choices.why: That describes an anion such as trichloromethanide, a carbene precursor.

choices.text: A neutral, stable molecule whose carbon has a full octet
choices.why: A carbene carbon has only six valence electrons, so carbenes are highly reactive and not isolable.

explanation: A carbene, R2C:, is a neutral molecule containing a divalent carbon with only six electrons in its valence shell. It is highly reactive and generated only as a reaction intermediate, not as an isolable molecule.

prompt: How many electrons are in the valence shell of the divalent carbon in a carbene, R2C:?
explanation: The carbene carbon has two bonds (four electrons) and one lone pair (two electrons): six in all, two short of an octet. That makes carbenes electron-deficient and highly reactive.

prompt: Why do carbenes react with C=C bonds?

choices.text: They are electron-deficient electrophiles, and the C=C bond is nucleophilic
They are electron-rich nucleophiles that attack the alkene's carbons
choices.why: A carbene carbon has only six valence electrons, so carbenes are electrophiles.

choices.text: They are radicals that add to the alkene and start a chain reaction
choices.why: Carbene addition occurs in a single step without intermediates; it isn't a chain reaction.

choices.text: They are strong acids that protonate the alkene to form a carbocation
choices.why: Carbenes don't donate protons; they add their carbon to the double bond.

explanation: Because they're electron-deficient, carbenes behave as electrophiles and react with nucleophilic C=C bonds. The reaction occurs in a single step without intermediates and gives a cyclopropane.

choices.text: By treating chloroform, CHCl3, with a strong base such as KOH
By treating diiodomethane, CH2I2, with a zinc–copper mix
choices.why: That gives the Simmons–Smith carbenoid, ICH2ZnI, not dichlorocarbene.

choices.text: By treating chloroform with a strong acid such as H2SO4
choices.why: A base is needed to remove the proton from CHCl3.

choices.text: By adding chlorine, Cl2, to an alkene in an inert solvent
choices.why: That gives a 1,2-dichloride.

explanation: Loss of a proton from CHCl3, caused by a strong base, gives the trichloromethanide anion, ^−:CCl3, which spontaneously expels Cl− to give dichlorocarbene.

prompt: In the formation of dichlorocarbene from CHCl3 and base, what does the trichloromethanide anion, ^−:CCl3, do?

choices.text: It spontaneously expels a chloride ion, Cl−, leaving :CCl2
It adds directly to the alkene to give the cyclopropane
choices.why: The anion first loses Cl− to become dichlorocarbene, and that is what adds to the alkene.

choices.text: It loses a second proton to become a dianion
choices.why: ^−:CCl3 has no hydrogen left to lose.

choices.text: It combines with K+ to form a salt that is the carbene
choices.why: The carbene is neutral :CCl2, formed when the anion expels Cl−.

explanation: Deprotonation of CHCl3 by base gives the trichloromethanide anion, ^−:CCl3. This anion spontaneously expels Cl− to yield dichlorocarbene, :CCl2 (Figure 8.9.1).

prompt: How is the carbon atom in dichlorocarbene described?

choices.text: sp2-hybridized, with a vacant p orbital and a lone pair in the third sp2 lobe
sp3-hybridized, with two lone pairs in two of its sp3 orbitals
choices.why: The carbon is sp2. It has one lone pair, in an sp2 orbital, and an empty p orbital.

choices.text: sp-hybridized and linear, with two empty p orbitals and no lone pairs
choices.why: The carbon is sp2 and carries a lone pair.

choices.text: sp2-hybridized, with a lone pair in the p orbital and an empty sp2 lobe
choices.why: It's the other way around: the p orbital is vacant and the lone pair occupies an sp2 lobe.

explanation: The carbon in dichlorocarbene is sp2-hybridized. A vacant p orbital extends above and below the plane of the three atoms, and an unshared pair of electrons occupies the third sp2 lobe.

prompt: In what way is dichlorocarbene similar to a carbocation such as CH3+?

choices.text: Both have an sp2-hybridized carbon with a vacant p orbital
Both carry a full positive charge on the carbon atom
choices.why: Dichlorocarbene is neutral. The similarity is the sp2 carbon and empty p orbital.

choices.text: Both have a lone pair of electrons in a carbon sp2 orbital
choices.why: The carbocation has no lone pair; dichlorocarbene does.

choices.text: Both have a carbon with a full octet of valence electrons
choices.why: Neither has an octet; the similarity is the sp2 carbon with an empty p orbital.

explanation: Dichlorocarbene resembles a carbocation in both the sp2 hybridization of carbon and the vacant p orbital. Electrostatic potential maps show a positive region at the empty p orbital in both; the carbene also has a negative region at its lone pair.

prompt: Addition of dichlorocarbene to an alkene is stereospecific. What does that mean?

choices.text: A single stereoisomer forms, keeping the alkene's cis or trans geometry
A cis alkene gives only the trans cyclopropane, and a trans alkene only the cis
choices.why: The alkene's geometry is kept, not reversed.

choices.text: Cis and trans alkenes both give the same mixture of cyclopropanes
choices.why: Only one stereoisomer forms, and it matches the alkene's geometry.

choices.text: The carbene bonds only to the less substituted double-bond carbon
choices.why: The carbene carbon bonds to both alkene carbons. Stereospecific refers to keeping the alkene's geometry.

explanation: Stereospecific means only a single stereoisomer is formed as product. Starting from a cis alkene, only the cis-disubstituted cyclopropane is produced; from a trans alkene, only the trans-disubstituted cyclopropane.

prompt: What product forms when cis-2-pentene reacts with CHCl3 and KOH?

choices.text: cis-1,1-Dichloro-2-ethyl-3-methylcyclopropane
trans-1,1-Dichloro-2-ethyl-3-methylcyclopropane
choices.why: The addition is stereospecific: a cis alkene gives only the cis cyclopropane.

choices.text: A mixture of cis- and trans-1,1-dichloro-2-ethyl-3-methylcyclopropane
choices.why: Only a single stereoisomer forms.

choices.text: 2,3-Dichloropentane
choices.why: That would come from adding Cl2. Dichlorocarbene adds a CCl2 carbon, forming a three-membered ring.

explanation: Dichlorocarbene adds its CCl2 carbon to both double-bond carbons, forming a cyclopropane. Because the addition is stereospecific, the ethyl and methyl groups keep their cis relationship.

prompt: What product would you expect from trans-2-butene with CHCl3 and KOH?

choices.text: trans-1,1-Dichloro-2,3-dimethylcyclopropane
cis-1,1-Dichloro-2,3-dimethylcyclopropane
choices.why: A trans alkene gives only the trans-disubstituted cyclopropane.

choices.text: A 50:50 mixture of the cis and trans cyclopropanes
choices.why: The addition is stereospecific; only one stereoisomer forms.

choices.text: 1,1-Dichloro-2,2-dimethylcyclopropane
choices.why: The methyl groups stay on separate carbons, as they were in the alkene.

explanation: Dichlorocarbene addition is stereospecific. From a trans alkene, only the trans-disubstituted cyclopropane forms, with the two methyl groups on opposite faces of the new ring.

prompt: In the Simmons–Smith reaction, what reagent forms from CH2I2 and zinc–copper, and what does it do?

choices.text: ICH2ZnI, (iodomethyl)zinc iodide, which transfers CH2 to the alkene
Free methylene, :CH2, which adds to the alkene as a carbene
choices.why: The Simmons–Smith reaction does not involve a free carbene; it uses a carbenoid.

choices.text: Dichlorocarbene, :CCl2, which gives a dichlorocyclopropane
choices.why: Dichlorocarbene comes from CHCl3 and KOH. Simmons–Smith gives nonhalogenated cyclopropanes.

choices.text: Zinc iodide, ZnI2, which adds an iodine to each alkene carbon
choices.why: ZnI2 is a by-product. The reagent transfers a CH2 group, not iodine, to the alkene.

explanation: Diiodomethane and a specially prepared zinc–copper mix give (iodomethyl)zinc iodide, ICH2ZnI. In the presence of an alkene, it transfers a CH2 group to the double bond to give a cyclopropane. It is the best method for nonhalogenated cyclopropanes.

choices.text: A metal-complexed reagent with carbene-like reactivity
A free carbene stabilized by the solvent
choices.why: A carbenoid isn't a free carbene; it is complexed to a metal.

choices.text: A cyclopropane that contains a metal atom
choices.why: A carbenoid is the reagent, not the product.

choices.text: Any carbene with halogen substituents, such as :CCl2
choices.why: Dichlorocarbene is a free carbene. A carbenoid, like ICH2ZnI, is complexed to a metal.

explanation: The Simmons–Smith reaction doesn't involve a free carbene. It uses a carbenoid, a metal-complexed reagent with carbene-like reactivity: ICH2ZnI, made from CH2I2 and zinc–copper.

prompt: What product forms when cyclohexene reacts with CH2I2 and a zinc–copper mix?

choices.text: Bicyclo[4.1.0]heptane, a cyclopropane ring fused to the cyclohexane ring
7,7-Dichlorobicyclo[4.1.0]heptane, with a CCl2 group across the ring bond
choices.why: A CCl2 group would come from CHCl3 and KOH. The Simmons–Smith reaction gives nonhalogenated cyclopropanes.

choices.text: Cycloheptene, with the CH2 inserted to enlarge the ring
choices.why: The CH2 bonds to both double-bond carbons to make a three-membered ring; it isn't inserted into the ring.

choices.text: trans-1,2-Diiodocyclohexane, from anti addition of iodine
choices.why: No iodine is added to the alkene; the zinc reagent transfers a CH2 group.

explanation: ICH2ZnI transfers a CH2 group to cyclohexene's double bond, giving bicyclo[4.1.0]heptane in 92% yield, along with ZnI2.

prompt: Methylenecyclohexane, C7H12 (a cyclohexane ring carbon double-bonded to CH2), reacts with CHCl3 and KOH. How many carbon atoms does the dichlorocyclopropane product contain?
explanation: Dichlorocarbene, :CCl2, adds its carbon across the C=C bond, so the product has the alkene's 7 carbons plus 1 from the carbene: 8 (C8H12Cl2). The new cyclopropane ring is made of the ring carbon, the former CH2 and the CCl2 carbon.

prompt: What product forms when 5-methyl-2-hexene, CH3CH=CHCH2CH(CH3)2, reacts with CH2I2 and zinc–copper?

choices.text: A cyclopropane with CH3 on one ring carbon and CH2CH(CH3)2 on the adjacent one
A cyclopropane with CH3 and CH2CH(CH3)2 on adjacent carbons and two Cl on the third
choices.why: No chlorine is involved; ICH2ZnI transfers a plain CH2 group.

choices.text: An open-chain alkene with one extra CH2 inserted between carbons 2 and 3
choices.why: The CH2 bonds to both double-bond carbons and forms a three-membered ring; no double bond remains.

choices.text: The diiodide CH3CHICHICH2CH(CH3)2, with iodine on carbons 2 and 3
choices.why: The iodines end up in ZnI2; only a CH2 group is transferred to the alkene.

explanation: The CH2 group bonds to both former double-bond carbons (carbons 2 and 3), forming a cyclopropane ring. One ring carbon keeps the original CH3 group and the other keeps the CH2CH(CH3)2 group.
